content: 1. As the mother’s breast milk production increases, the infant should be fed approximately 60 ml per day. 2. If an infant refuses or is reluctant to breastfeed, the primary reasons may include illness, pain, or sedation. 3. If the infant is able to suckle, encourage the mother to breastfeed more frequently. 4. If the infant is severely ill, the mother may need to express breast milk and feed the infant using a cup or gastric tube until breastfeeding can resume. 5. If the infant is hospitalized, arrangements should be made for the mother to stay with the infant to facilitate breastfeeding. 6. Assist the mother in finding a comfortable way to hold the infant without putting pressure on painful areas. 7. Teach the mother how to clear a blocked nose, as this can interfere with feeding. Suggest shorter, more frequent feeds for a few days. 8. A sore mouth in the infant may be caused by a Candida infection (thrush) or teething. Treat thrush with nystatin suspension (100,000 U/ml), administering 1–2 ml into the mouth four times daily for 7 days. If nystatin is unavailable, apply a 1% gentian violet solution. 9. Encourage the mother of a teething infant to remain patient and continue offering the breast. 10. If the mother is on regular sedation, consider reducing the dose or switching to a less sedating alternative. 11. If breastfeeding technique is problematic, assist the mother in ensuring proper positioning and attachment of the infant without pressing on the infant’s head or shaking the breast. 12. Advise against the use of feeding bottles or pacifiers; if necessary, use a cup for feeding. 13. Treat breast engorgement by removing milk from the breast to prevent mastitis or abscess formation. If the infant cannot suckle, help the mother express her milk. 14. If there is an oversupply of milk due to ineffective suckling or frequent feeding, help the mother manage the oversupply. Oversupply can also occur if the mother unnecessarily feeds from both breasts at each session. 15. Changes such as separation from the mother, a new caregiver, maternal illness, changes in family routine, or alterations in the mother’s scent (e.g., due to different soap, food, or menstruation) can upset the infant and lead to breastfeeding refusal. 16. Low-birth-weight infants (<2.5 kg) require breast milk even more than larger infants but may not be able to breastfeed immediately after birth, especially if they are very small. 17. For the first few days, such infants may need to be fed intravenously if oral feeding is not possible. 18. Begin early feeding with small oral feeds as soon as the infant can tolerate enteral feeding, even on the first day. 19. Infants weighing <1.5 kg may require feeding via a nasogastric or orogastric tube during the initial days of life. 20. Preferably, feed the infant with the mother’s expressed breast milk. 21. The mother can allow the infant to suck on her cleaned finger while being tube-fed to stimulate the digestive tract and promote weight gain. 22. Low-birth-weight infants at ≥32 weeks’ gestational age can begin suckling at the breast. Encourage the mother to put the infant to the breast as soon as the infant is well enough. 23. Continue providing expressed breast milk via cup or tube to ensure the infant receives adequate nutrition. 24. Infants at ≥34–36 weeks’ gestational age can usually take all their nutritional needs directly from the breast. 25. Non-breastfed infants should receive either expressed breast milk (preferably from their own mother or donor human milk from safe and affordable milk-banking facilities), formula milk prepared with clean water according to instructions, or ready-made liquid formula. 26. If none of the above options are available, consider animal milk. Dilute cow’s milk by adding 50 ml of water to 100 ml of milk, then add 10 g of sugar and an approved micronutrient supplement. Avoid using this for premature infants. 27. For infants weighing <2.0 kg, provide 150 ml/kg daily, divided into eight feeds at 3-hour intervals. 28. If the child is too weak to suck but can swallow, feeding can be done with a cup. 29. If the child is lethargic, severely anorexic, or unable to swallow, feed via a nasogastric or orogastric tube. 30. For sick children, continue breastfeeding and do not withhold food. 31. Provide frequent, small feeds every 2–3 hours, coaxing and encouraging the child patiently. 32. If the child is severely anorexic, feed via a nasogastric tube. 33. Promote catch-up growth after the child’s appetite returns. 34. The food provided should be palatable, easily eaten (soft or liquid consistency), easily digested, and rich in energy and nutrients. 35. The basic principle of nutritional management is to provide a diet with sufficient energy-producing foods and high-quality proteins. Foods with high oil or fat content are recommended, with up to 30–40% of total calories from fat. 36. Feeding at frequent intervals is necessary to achieve high energy intake. 37. For sick children, provide multivitamin and mineral supplements. 38. Encourage the child to eat relatively small amounts frequently. 39. If young children are left to feed themselves or must compete with siblings for food, they may not get enough to eat. 40. A blocked nose with dry or thick mucus may interfere with feeding. Use saline drops or a moistened wick to soften the mucus. 41. Recipes for catch-up meals should provide 100 kcal and 3 g protein per 100 ml. Individual servings should contain approximately 200 kcal and 6 g protein. A child should eat seven meals in 24 hours. 42. Recipe 1 (porridge without milk): Combine 100 g cereal flour, 100 g groundnut or oilseed paste, and 50 g sugar. Make a thick porridge, stir in the paste and sugar, and make up to 1 liter. 43. Recipe 2 (porridge with milk or rice pudding): Combine 125 g cereal flour, 600 ml milk, 75 g sugar, and 25 g oil or margarine. Make a thick porridge with milk and a little water, then add sugar and oil. Make up to 1 liter. 44. Recipe 3 (rice-based meal): Combine 75 g rice, 50 g lentils, 75 g pumpkin, 75 g green leaves, 25 g oil or margarine, and 800 ml water. Cook with a lid on, adding chopped leaves just before the rice is cooked. Cook for a few more minutes. 45. Recipe 4 (rice-based meal with cooked family foods): Combine 90 g cooked rice, 30 g cooked mashed beans, peas, or lentils, 30 g cooked mashed pumpkin, and 10 g margarine or oil. Soften the mashed foods with oil or margarine. 46. Recipe 5 (maize-based meal with family foods): Combine 140 g thick maize porridge, 15 g groundnut paste, 30 g egg, and 20 g green leaves. Stir groundnut paste and raw egg into cooked porridge, cook for a few minutes, and add fried onion, tomato, and leaves for flavor. 47. During illness, feed children more frequently than usual, offering at least one additional meal per day after their appetite increases. 48. Monitor fluid intake carefully in very sick children, ensuring adequate hydration. 49. Prefer oral fluids (by mouth or nasogastric tube) over intravenous fluids. 50. If IV fluids are necessary, monitor the infusion closely to avoid fluid overload, which can lead to heart failure or cerebral edema. 51. Use IV fluids only for severe dehydration, septic shock, IV antibiotic delivery, or when oral fluids are contraindicated. 52. Possible IV maintenance fluids include half-normal saline with 5% or 10% glucose. Avoid using 5% glucose alone, as it can cause hyponatremia. 53. Fever is not an automatic indication for antibiotics and may support immune defense against infection. 54. Treat fever with paracetamol (15 mg/kg every 6 hours) or ibuprofen (10 mg/kg every 6–8 hours) if the child is uncomfortable or distressed. 55. Avoid aspirin as a first-line antipyretic due to its association with Reye syndrome.
